phil:epictetus: Epictetus was a Greek Stoic philosopher who was born into slavery and later won his freedom to teach in Rome and then Nicopolis. He left no writings of his own; his teachings survive through the Discourses and the compact Enchiridion, both recorded by his student Arrian. His central lesson is the dichotomy of control: some things are up to us, chiefly our judgments and choices, while externals such as health, reputation, and possessions are not, and tranquility comes from disciplining our desires to the former alone.
phil:seneca: Seneca the Younger was a Roman Stoic philosopher, statesman, and dramatist who served for a time as tutor and advisor to the emperor Nero, before being forced to take his own life. He is best known for his Letters to Lucilius and a series of moral essays on topics such as anger, the shortness of life, and how to face adversity. His writing translates Stoic ethics into vivid practical counsel, urging readers to use time well, master destructive emotions, and remain indifferent to fortune's swings.
phil:marcus-aurelius: Marcus Aurelius was Roman emperor from 161 to 180 and the last of the so-called Five Good Emperors, remembered as much for his philosophy as for his reign. During military campaigns he kept a private notebook, later known as the Meditations, written in Greek as a series of reflections addressed to himself. Drawing on Stoic thought, these entries counsel acceptance of nature's order, dutiful service to the common good, and equanimity in the face of hardship and mortality.
phil:cicero: Marcus Tullius Cicero was a Roman statesman, orator, and philosopher whose works became a principal channel through which Greek philosophy reached the Latin-speaking world. Though not a systematic thinker of one school, he drew on Academic skepticism, Stoicism, and other traditions in dialogues such as On Duties, On the Nature of the Gods, and On the Ends of Good and Evil. He is especially known for his defense of natural law, republican virtue, and a life guided by moral duty, and his polished Latin prose shaped European rhetoric for centuries.
phil:lucretius: Lucretius was a Roman poet and philosopher whose single surviving work, the epic poem On the Nature of Things, presents the physics and ethics of Epicureanism in verse. He argued that the universe is composed of atoms moving through void, that natural phenomena have material rather than divine causes, and that the soul dies with the body. His aim was therapeutic: by showing that the gods do not meddle in human affairs and that death is nothing to us, he hoped to free readers from fear and superstition.
phil:plotinus: Plotinus was a philosopher of the Roman era and the founder of Neoplatonism, whose lectures were collected by his student Porphyry into the six sets of treatises known as the Enneads. Building on Plato, he described reality as a hierarchy emanating from a single ineffable source he called the One, from which proceed Intellect and Soul, and ultimately the material world. He held that the human soul can ascend back toward its origin through contemplation, culminating in a mystical union with the One, an idea that deeply influenced later Christian, Islamic, and Jewish thought.
phil:confucius: Confucius was a Chinese teacher and philosopher of the late Zhou period whose ideas, gathered by disciples in the Analects, became the foundation of the Confucian tradition. He emphasized moral self-cultivation, ritual propriety, and the virtue of ren, often rendered as humaneness or benevolence, as the basis of a well-ordered family, society, and state. Rather than metaphysical speculation, his concern was the practical shaping of character and proper conduct within human relationships, and his teachings profoundly shaped East Asian ethics, education, and government.
phil:mencius: Mencius was a Chinese Confucian philosopher of the Warring States period regarded as the most important early interpreter of Confucius. He is best known for arguing that human nature is inherently good, illustrated by the spontaneous alarm anyone feels on seeing a child about to fall into a well, and that moral virtues grow from innate sprouts that education and reflection can nurture. He also developed influential political ideas, holding that rulers govern by a mandate contingent on the people's welfare and that a tyrant forfeits his right to rule.
phil:xunzi: Xunzi was a Chinese Confucian philosopher of the Warring States period who offered a rigorous, systematic defense and revision of Confucian thought. In sharp contrast to Mencius, he argued that human nature is bad, or at least unruly, and that goodness is a deliberate achievement produced by education, ritual, and social institutions that reshape our raw desires. He gave a naturalistic account of Heaven as impersonal nature rather than a moral agent, and his emphasis on order through cultivation influenced later Chinese thought, including his students associated with Legalism.
phil:laozi: Laozi is the semi-legendary figure traditionally credited with founding Daoism and authoring the Dao De Jing, a short and enigmatic classic of Chinese philosophy. The text centers on the Dao, the ineffable way or source underlying all things, and commends living in harmony with it through simplicity, humility, and wu wei, or effortless non-forcing action. Its paradoxical aphorisms counsel yielding rather than striving and value the natural and spontaneous over rigid convention, shaping Chinese religion, art, and political thought for millennia.
phil:zhuangzi: Zhuangzi was a Chinese Daoist philosopher of the Warring States period whose eponymous book is celebrated for its wit, parables, and literary imagination. He extended Daoist thought toward a playful skepticism about fixed distinctions, questioning the boundaries between right and wrong, dream and waking, and self and world, as in his famous doubt over whether he was a man dreaming he was a butterfly. He championed spontaneity, freedom from conventional values, and acceptance of transformation and death as part of the natural flow of the Dao.
phil:sun-tzu: Sun Tzu is the name traditionally given to the author of The Art of War, an ancient Chinese treatise on military strategy composed around the Warring States era. The work presents warfare as a discipline governed by calculation, deception, terrain, and timing, holding that the highest skill lies in winning without fighting by subduing an enemy through superior positioning and foresight. Though a manual of strategy rather than a philosophical system, its aphorisms on adaptability, self-knowledge, and knowing one's opponent have been widely applied far beyond the battlefield.
phil:buddha: The Buddha, born Siddhartha Gautama, was an Indian teacher and the founder of Buddhism, who according to tradition renounced a princely life to seek release from suffering and attained awakening under the Bodhi tree. His core teaching is the Four Noble Truths: that life involves suffering, that suffering arises from craving, that it can cease, and that the Eightfold Path leads to that cessation, or nirvana. He rejected both indulgence and severe asceticism in favor of a middle way, and taught that all things are impermanent and lack a permanent self.
phil:nagarjuna: Nagarjuna was an Indian Buddhist philosopher and founder of the Madhyamaka, or Middle Way, school of Mahayana thought. He is best known for the doctrine of emptiness, the claim that all phenomena lack any independent, intrinsic nature because they arise only in dependence on other things. Through rigorous dialectical arguments, developed most famously in his Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way, he sought to dissolve metaphysical extremes and fixed views while avoiding nihilism, an approach that profoundly shaped later Buddhist philosophy across Asia.
phil:dogen: Dogen was a Japanese Zen master of the Kamakura period who founded the Soto school of Zen in Japan after studying Chan Buddhism in China. He is best known for his teaching of shikantaza, or just sitting, and for the radical claim that zazen is not a means to enlightenment but its very expression, so that practice and realization are one. His major work, the Shobogenzo, explores subtle themes of time, being, and impermanence in dense and poetic prose, and remains a landmark of Japanese religious philosophy.
